Q: (docker, nvidia-ctk) error while loading shared libraries: libcuda.so.1: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory A:

This is a classic driver vs. runtime mismatch issue. Your host has CUDA 12.0 (driver 525.60.13), but your container is pulling CUDA 13.1.0-devel libraries, which aren’t compatible with the older driver.

The root cause: libcuda.so.1 is the driver library. It’s not inside the container—it’s mounted from the host by the NVIDIA container toolkit. When you use a CUDA image newer than your driver supports, the container’s CUDA runtime expects a newer libcuda.so.1 than what’s available.

Fix:

  1. Use a CUDA image matching your host CUDA version:
    Change your FROM to:

    dockerfile

    FROM nvidia/cuda:12.0.1-devel-ubuntu22.04

    Your driver 525.60.13 supports CUDA 12.0, not 13.1.

  2. Remove all manual ENV adjustments for library paths—the NVIDIA base image already sets these correctly. You’re likely breaking the toolkit’s mounts.

  3. Test with a minimal image first:

    bash

    docker run --gpus all --rm nvidia/cuda:12.0.1-base-ubuntu22.04 nvidia-smi

    Then:

    bash

    docker run --gpus all --rm nvidia/cuda:12.0.1-devel-ubuntu22.04 bash -c "ldconfig -p | grep libcuda"

  4. For the NVRTC error: That’s likely because Futhark is compiling for a newer GPU architecture than your A100 supports. Check your CUDA image’s default -arch flag. The A100 is sm_80. You may need to pass -arch=sm_80 to nvcc or futhark cuda.

Why the pytorch image works: It’s CUDA 10.1, which is older than your driver—so backward compatibility kicks in.

TL;DR:

  • Downgrade your base image to nvidia/cuda:12.0.1-devel-ubuntu22.04.

  • Strip the custom ENV lines—they’re overriding the NVIDIA container’s correct paths.

  • The NVRTC error is separate and likely an architecture flag issue.

On a side note, debugging dependency chains like this reminds me of working on puzzle solvers—one wrong constraint and the whole system breaks.

Q: How to get the expansions from a glob pattern to use in another path A:

I think that you could do something with regex, not sure about the exceptions.

One start point could be this (actually it only prints the result path for your example):

import re

a='./a/**/foo/**/*.json'
new=r'./new/\2/\1/\3.txt'
b='./a/b/c/foo/bar/bat/test.json'
a=re.escape(a)
m1=re.match(r"[^\\\*]+",a) #non * chars
r1=re.compile(r"(?<!\\\*)\\\*(?!\\\*)") #one * char

a=r1.sub("([^/]*)",a)
a=a.replace("\\*\\*","(.*?)")
r2=re.compile(a)

str =re.sub(r2,new,b)
print(str)

Take a look at the source code:

Function translate / Glob

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/3.14/Lib/glob.py#L273

Function _translate / Fnmatch

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/3.14/Lib/fnmatch.py#L109

I was playing with glob.translate and it output this regex for your example:

(?s:\./a/(?:[^/.][^/]*/)*foo/(?:[^/.][^/]*/)*(?!\.)[^/]*\.json)\Z

If someone could change the code to include the ?: groups inside a group, then one could recover it value:

(?s:\./a/((?:[^/.][^/]*/)*)foo/((?:[^/.][^/]*/)*)(?!\.)([^/]*)\.json)\Z

Also [^/]* need to be inside a group. I tried to manage any/one_segments constants of the glob.translate function, but only one part was grouped. I think the problem could go inside the fnmatch._translate function.

Q: Salesforce CLI access-token fails due to token SF_ACCESS_TOKEN format A:

The issue is likely the exclamation mark ! inside your double quotes.

In most terminals (like bash or zsh), ! is a special character that tries to search your command history. So when you run that export command with double quotes, the terminal is likely scrambling your token or trying to "expand" it before the Salesforce CLI even sees it.

Just use single quotes '' instead. Single quotes tell the terminal to treat the string exactly as it is, without changing anything.

Try this:

export SF_ACCESS_TOKEN='00DSB00000ltHQA2A2!theAccessToken'

Once you export it with single quotes, try the login command again. It should work perfectly.

Q: How to improve NLTK sentence segmentation? A:

The awesome-ness of Kiss and Strunk (2006) Punkt algorithm is that it's unsupervised. So given a new text, you should retrain the model and apply the model to your text, e.g. 

>>> from nltk.tokenize.punkt import PunktSentenceTokenizer, PunktParameters
>>> text = "An ambitious campus expansion plan was proposed by Fr. Vernon F. Gallagher in 1952. Assumption Hall, the first student dormitory, was opened in 1954, and Rockwell Hall was dedicated in November 1958, housing the schools of business and law. It was during the tenure of F. Henry J. McAnulty that Fr. Gallagher's ambitious plans were put to action."

# Training a new model with the text.
>>> tokenizer = PunktSentenceTokenizer()
>>> tokenizer.train(text)
<nltk.tokenize.punkt.PunktParameters object at 0x106c5d828>

# It automatically learns the abbreviations.
>>> tokenizer._params.abbrev_types
{'f', 'fr', 'j'}

# Use the customized tokenizer.
>>> tokenizer.tokenize(text)
['An ambitious campus expansion plan was proposed by Fr. Vernon F. Gallagher in 1952.', 'Assumption Hall, the first student dormitory, was opened in 1954, and Rockwell Hall was dedicated in November 1958, housing the schools of business and law.', "It was during the tenure of F. Henry J. McAnulty that Fr. Gallagher's ambitious plans were put to action."]

Where there's not enough data to generate good statistics when re-training the model, you can also put in a pre-determined list of abbreviations before training; see How to avoid NLTK's sentence tokenizer spliting on abbreviations?

>>> from nltk.tokenize.punkt import PunktSentenceTokenizer, PunktParameters

>>> punkt_param = PunktParameters()
>>> abbreviation = ['f', 'fr', 'k']
>>> punkt_param.abbrev_types = set(abbreviation)

>>> tokenizer = PunktSentenceTokenizer(punkt_param)
>>> tokenizer.train(text)
<nltk.tokenize.punkt.PunktParameters object at 0x106c5d828>

>>> tokenizer.tokenize(text)
['An ambitious campus expansion plan was proposed by Fr. Vernon F. Gallagher in 1952.', 'Assumption Hall, the first student dormitory, was opened in 1954, and Rockwell Hall was dedicated in November 1958, housing the schools of business and law.', "It was during the tenure of F. Henry J. McAnulty that Fr. Gallagher's ambitious plans were put to action."]

Q: Printing all records of a student who failed one subject A:

You can do it using SUM OVER() clause as follows :

This does the group by Student_id. And it calculates the number of failed object using SUM CASE clause

with cte as (
  select *, sum(case when marks <50 then 1 else 0 end) over (partition by Student_id) as failed
  from student
)
select Student_id, name, subject, marks
from cte
where failed >= 1

Q: watchOS SwiftUI: UI redraws are delayed in Always-On / power-saving mode despite active timer A:

SwiftUI redraw throttling in always-on/power-saving mode is intentional and unavoidable watchOS system behavior. While your app continues executing (including timers and workout sessions) the system significantly reduces or defers UI rendering to save power.

There is no supported API to maintain a consistent SwiftUI update frequency while the display is dimmed; foreground execution and workout mode don't override this limitation.

What you could do instead is design the UI to be time-derived rather than update driven. Use TimelineView, timestamps or clock-based calculations so the UI reflects the correct state whenever the system allows a redraw, rather than assuming every timer tick will be rendered. You could also adapt UI fidelity using isLuminanceReduced.
